screens.title: SQLAlchemy ORM — Models and Basic Operations
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll make the shift from SQLAlchemy Core's table-and-column world to the ORM, where rows are ordinary Python objects. You'll learn why mapping classes to tables speeds development, how declarative_base establishes that mapping, and how the Session manages a unit of work so your object changes become S Q L transactions. We'll walk through defining a simple User model, creating tables from models, and then performing the full CRUD lifecycle — add, query, update, and delete — all with safe session management. Along the way we'll surface common misconceptions: thinking a queried object is magically persistent across separate sessions, or relying on flush without a commit. By the end you'll be comfortable creating models, using sessionmaker, and grouping related operations into a single transaction. A short hands-on activity will ask you to implement a Book model and exercise one CRUD operation so you can practice the pattern with an SQLite file. This foundation prepares you for relationships and richer object graphs in later chapters. Ready to translate S Q L into objects and write clearer, more maintainable database code?

Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › SQLAlchemy ORM Overview
SQLAlchemy ORM — Models and Basic Operations
Object-centric database access with declarative models and sessions.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson
Define models, run CRUD, and manage sessions safely.
Core focus
declarative_base, Session, commit vs rollback.
Outcome
You can map classes and run reliable transactions.
Quick orientation
Why this matters

Working with objects instead of raw SQL brings your business logic and data model into the same language. It reduces boilerplate SQL and makes maintenance easier as your application grows.

Common pitfall

Objects live inside a Session. Expecting object state to persist across different sessions without reattaching is a frequent source of confusion.

Visual concept
Class → Row
A declarative class defines columns and the tablename. Creating an instance means a new row is staged in a session.
Explore Key Topics
Models & declarative_base()
Establish class-to-table mappings and metadata for table creation.
Session & sessionmaker
Manage a unit of work: staging, flushing, committing, or rolling back changes.
CRUD patterns
Add objects, query them, update attributes, and delete with explicit commits.
Starter Activity

Define a Book model, create the table, and add three rows in an SQLite file. Verify results with queries.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your work with SQLAlchemy's ORM. First, you'll be able to name the difference between Core and ORM and explain why ORM improves developer productivity by mapping rows to objects. Second, you'll define Python classes as ORM models using declarative_base, including columns and tablename so your classes match the database layout. Third, you'll create and use a Session via sessionmaker to stage changes and run transactional work, knowing when to commit or rollback. Finally, you'll practice CRUD: add new model instances, query them with filter and get calls, update attributes to generate update statements, and delete records safely. For each objective you'll both read and run example code and verify results, so you not only understand the A P I but also can reason about session scope and state. These skills matter because they let you organize data logic in Python, avoid repetitive S Q L, and reduce bugs tied to improper session handling.

screens.title: SQLAlchemy Core vs ORM
screens.narratorSegment: Start by clarifying the practical difference between Core and ORM. SQLAlchemy Core exposes tables, columns, and S Q L expressions; you construct SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE with engine-level execution. The ORM layers an object mapping on top: Python classes become table blueprints and instances represent rows. Use Core when you need fine-grained S Q L control, complex multi-table expressions, or want to stay close to S Q L. Use ORM when you prefer to manipulate Python objects, encapsulate domain logic in classes, and reduce repetitive S Q L. A common example: inserting many rows with Core can be efficient for bulk operations, while ORM is clearer for a domain model where business rules belong on class methods. Watch for a misconception: ORM does not replace S Q L — understanding generated S Q L helps debug performance. A good habit is to inspect emitted S Q L during development to ensure queries are optimal. Practice contrast: write a small SELECT in both styles and observe how Core focuses on table objects while ORM returns class instances you can pass around in your application. Which approach fits your problem depends on clarity, control, and performance trade-offs.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Core vs ORM
SQLAlchemy Core (table-centric)
You construct SQL expressions using Table objects, Column definitions, and compile those expressions. Execution happens against an Engine and returns raw rows or result proxies.
When to use
  • Complex SQL, fine tuning, bulk insert performance.
  • When you need explicit control over joins and SQL functions.
Misconception

Choosing ORM doesn't remove SQL knowledge; it just shifts the interface. Inspect generated SQL when debugging performance.

SQLAlchemy ORM (object-centric)
Define classes that inherit from a declarative base. Instances map to rows, and the Session manages persistence, change tracking, and transactions.
When to use
  • Domain models, business logic on classes, clearer application code.
  • When maintainability and readability are priorities.
Misconception

ORM does not automatically optimize every query; inefficient patterns can still produce heavy SQL. Learn query methods and session behavior.

Key Takeaway

Both Core and ORM are valuable. Use Core for SQL control, ORM for object-oriented application code. Understanding both gives you flexibility.

screens.title: declarative_base() and Declarative Models
screens.narratorSegment: The declarative base is the foundation of the ORM mapping. Calling declarative_base produces a Base class that collects metadata and mapping information. When your model classes inherit from this Base and set tablename and Column attributes, SQLAlchemy registers the mapping between Python attributes and table columns. Concretely, you declare id as a Column with Integer and primary_key=True and name as a Column with String and not-null constraints; these definitions are both Python attributes and schema descriptors. One practical effect: when you call Base. metadata. create_all(engine), SQLAlchemy inspects the registered metadata and creates tables for each mapped class. A useful example is a User class with id, name, and email; after you instantiate Base and define User, creating tables is a one-line call. A common misconception is that simply defining classes writes tables — you must call create_all or use migrations to apply schema. Also remember that Column objects belong to class attributes, not instance attributes; instances receive values at runtime. How would you design your next model to represent application logic cleanly? declarative_base() and Declarative Models means inherit from base to register models; column class attributes become schema and mapping descriptors used by create_all and queries.. In practical terms, how a base class turns python classes into mapped tables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Declarative Base
Core concept

declarative_base creates a Base class that stores table mappings and metadata. Models that inherit from Base are registered automatically.

Model anatomy
  • __tablename__: explicit table name string.
  • Column attributes: Column(Integer), Column(String(...)).
  • Optional __repr__ to aid debugging.
Misconception

Defining a model does not modify the database until you run create_all or apply migrations. Model code alone is inert with respect to the DB schema.

Example model
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base
from sqlalchemy import Column, Integer, String

Base = declarative_base()

class User(Base):
  __tablename__ = 'users'
  id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
  name = Column(String(50), nullable=False)
  email = Column(String(100), unique=True, nullable=False)

  def __repr__(self):
    return f"<User(id={'{'}self.id{'}'}, name='{'{'}self.name{'}'}', email='{'{'}self.email{'}'}')>"
Call Base.metadata.create_all(engine) to create tables for registered models.
Key Takeaway

declarative_base is the registry for model mappings. Define Column attributes on classes and then explicitly create tables when ready.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Model & Create Tables
Starter code
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, Column, Integer, String
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base

engine = create_engine('sqlite:///orm_example.db')
Base = declarative_base()

class User(Base):
  __tablename__ = 'users'
  id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
  name = Column(String(50), nullable=False)
  email = Column(String(100), unique=True, nullable=False)

Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
print("Table 'users' created or already exists via ORM model.")
Explanation & check
  • create_engine sets up the DB connection object used for DDL and DML.
  • Base.metadata.create_all(engine) inspects Base's registry and issues CREATE TABLE where missing.
  • create_all will not migrate existing tables — use migrations for schema evolution.
Pro tip
Run create_all in development or tests. In production, prefer migrations to manage schema changes safely.
Key Takeaway

Defining models and calling create_all gives you a quick way to materialize tables during development. For production changes, use migrations.

screens.title: Session and sessionmaker
screens.narratorSegment: The Session is the ORM's conversation partner for the database. It tracks object state, stages new objects for insertion, notes attribute changes for updates, and marks objects for deletion. To obtain sessions you create a sessionmaker factory bound to an engine; calling that factory returns a new Session instance. Treat a session as a short-lived unit of work: open it, perform related operations, then commit or rollback and close it. The best practice is to use the with-statement so Python closes the session automatically even if an exception occurs. This pattern prevents connection leaks and makes error handling explicit. Remember the difference between flush and commit: flush writes pending S Q L to the database but keeps the transaction open; commit finalizes the transaction. A typical pattern is to add or modify several objects, call commit once, and then verify results. A misconception is assuming objects are sessionless — objects are attached to a session and carrying them across sessions without merging will produce errors or detached states. Always be explicit about session boundaries. Session and sessionmaker means create sessions with sessionmaker. use with-statement to ensure closure, commit to persist, rollback on error, and avoid carrying objects across different sessions without merging.. In practical terms, the session as a unit of work and how to obtain one. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Session & sessionmaker
What is a Session?

A Session tracks object states and translates those changes to SQL. It groups related operations into a transactional unit of work.

Best practice

Create a session factory via sessionmaker and prefer using: with Session() as session: so sessions are closed reliably.

Misconception
An object returned from one session is not automatically attached to another session. Reattach or requery before modifying in a different session.
Session factory example
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker

Session = sessionmaker(bind=engine)

with Session() as session:
  # work with session: add, query, commit
  new_user = User(name='Alice', email='alice@example.com')
  session.add(new_user)
  session.commit()
Key Takeaway

Treat sessions as short-lived units of work. Use sessionmaker and with blocks to manage lifecycle, commit to persist, and rollback on errors.

screens.title: CREATE — Adding Objects and Persisting
screens.narratorSegment: Creating new rows with the ORM is intuitive: instantiate your model class and add the instance to a Session. session. add stages a single object; session. add_all stages a list. When you commit, SQLAlchemy flushes pending INSERTs to the database and then commits the transaction so data is persistent. A concrete example: create a User instance and call session. add(new_user) then session. commit(); after commit the new_user. id will be populated if the primary key is auto-incrementing. A common misunderstanding is thinking flush equals commit — flush writes S Q L to the database but keeps the transaction open; a rollback can undo flushed changes before commit. Another pitfall is committing too often: many small commits can hurt performance compared to grouping related operations into one transaction. For bulk inserts you may prefer Core or use optimized ORM bulk methods for speed, but for typical application logic, add and commit inside a with Session() block offers clarity and safety. CREATE — Adding Objects and Persisting means use session.add or session.add_all to stage objects, then call commit to flush and finalize the transaction. avoid confusing flush with commit.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Create: Add & Commit
CREATE example
with Session() as session:
  new_user = User(name='Alice', email='alice@example.com')
  session.add(new_user)
  session.commit()
  print(f"Created user: {new_user}")

  # add multiple
  bob = User(name='Bob', email='bob@example.com')
  charlie = User(name='Charlie', email='charlie@example.com')
  session.add_all([bob, charlie])
  session.commit()
Notes & checks
  • After commit, auto-incremented IDs are populated on instances.
  • Use add_all to stage many objects for readability.
  • Avoid uncommitted sessions if you expect persistent changes across program runs.
Common mistake
Calling session.close without commit will discard pending changes if transaction not committed. Close only after commit or rollback.
Key Takeaway

Add objects to a session and commit once you are ready. Group related changes to reduce transaction overhead and avoid performance penalties.

screens.title: READ — Querying Objects with the Session
screens.narratorSegment: Reading data with the ORM is expressive and chainable. The most efficient primary-key retrieval uses session. get(Model, primary_key). For filtered queries, session. query(Model). filter_by(keyword=...) offers simple equality checks, while filter accepts S Q L expressions for richer conditions. You can use. first() to fetch one row or. all() to return a list. For example, query all users, print them, then select a user named Alice using filter_by(name='Alice'). To find users whose email domain matches, use filter with an S Q L expression such as Model. email. like. You can chain order_by to sort results; for example order_by(User. name. desc()) returns names in descending order. A misconception is expecting query results to be plain dictionaries — ORM returns model instances with attributes you can access directly. Also be mindful of lazy-loaded relationships in later chapters; those queries happen when you access the attribute. End your read routines with explicit checks rather than assuming results exist, and use get for efficient primary key access. READ — Querying Objects with the Session means use session.get for primary key lookups, query() plus filter/filter_by for conditions, and first()/all() to control result shape. chain order_by to sort results.. In practical terms, session.get, query(), filter_by(), filter(), first(), all(), and order_by(). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. with Session() as session:
  user_by_id = session.get(User, 1)

  • filter_by is convenient for equality checks; filter accepts SQL expressions for flexibility.

When performance matters, inspect generated SQL or use Core for complex sets. For many simple reads, ORM query methods are expressive and efficient.

Choose get for single primary-key fetches, filter/filter_by for conditions, and always verify query results rather than assuming existence.

screens.title: UPDATE — Changing Objects and Flushing Changes
screens.narratorSegment: Updating records in the ORM is intentionally simple because the Session tracks object state. Query the object you want to change, set new attribute values on the instance, then commit the session. SQLAlchemy will detect the attribute change and emit an UPDATE for the changed columns during flush. For example, find Bob by name, assign a new email value, and then call commit. After committing, a follow-up query verifies the persisted change. A common error is attempting to update an object that was queried in a different, now-closed session without reattaching it. In that case, either requery the object in the new session or merge the detached object. Another pitfall is making assumptions about transactional boundaries: changes remain local to the session until you commit. If you need atomic updates across multiple related objects, perform them inside the same session and then commit once so all changes succeed or all roll back together. This approach keeps your data consistent and your code easier to reason about. UPDATE — Changing Objects and Flushing Changes means modify attributes on a session-attached instance; the session tracks changes and emits update on commit. keep transactional changes grouped.. In practical terms, modify attributes, rely on change tracking, then commit. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Update: Object State
UPDATE example
with Session() as session:
  user_to_update = session.query(User).filter_by(name='Bob').first()
  if user_to_update:
    user_to_update.email = 'robert@example.com'
    session.commit()
    print(f"Updated Bob's email to: {user_to_update.email}")
  else:
    print('Bob not found for update.')
Notes & checkpoints
  • Session automatically detects attribute changes and generates UPDATE statements on flush/commit.
  • Requery or merge objects if you work across session boundaries.
  • Group related updates into a single commit to maintain atomicity.
Common mistake
Changing attributes on a detached object will not be persisted unless merged into a live session or reloaded from the DB.
Key Takeaway

Update by changing attributes on session-attached instances and commit. Avoid detached-object surprises by keeping clear session boundaries.

screens.title: DELETE — Marking for Deletion and Verification
screens.narratorSegment: To remove rows via the ORM, query the instance you want deleted, call session. delete(instance), then commit. Deletion marks the object for removal, and commit finalizes the change. Always perform a follow-up query to verify the row no longer exists. For example, find Charlie by name, call session. delete(user_to_delete), commit, and then query filter_by(name='Charlie') to confirm the result is None. Be careful with cascade behavior when you have related objects: deleting a parent may also remove children depending on your relationship configuration and database constraints. A common mistake is deleting an object in one session and then trying to inspect it as if it were still valid in that same in-memory reference; after commit the instance is usually considered deleted or expired. If deletion is conditional or reversible, prefer a status flag column rather than physical deletion so you preserve history. When you do perform hard deletes, group them in transactions and verify with queries. Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Delete: Remove Rows
DELETE example
with Session() as session:
  user_to_delete = session.query(User).filter_by(name='Charlie').first()
  if user_to_delete:
    session.delete(user_to_delete)
    session.commit()
    print(f"Deleted user: {user_to_delete}")

screens.title: commit(), flush(), rollback() — Transaction semantics
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding transaction semantics is vital. session. flush sends pending S Q L statements to the database without finalizing the transaction. It allows the database to assign values, like auto-incremented IDs, so your in-memory objects receive those values. session. commit flushes and then commits the transaction, making changes permanent. If an error occurs, session. rollback undoes pending changes in that session, returning a clean transactional state. A common mistake is expecting flush to make data durable — it does not; an uncommitted transaction can still be rolled back. Another mistake is calling commit too frequently: many small commits hurt throughput and increase overhead. The practical pattern is to group related changes into a single commit after successful validation. Using with Session() as session: also helps because it ensures the session is closed reliably; you should still explicitly commit or rollback as appropriate. When debugging, inspect the S Q L emitted during flush and commit to understand what the ORM translates from your object operations. commit(), flush(), rollback() — Transaction semantics means flush writes sql but leaves the transaction open. commit finalizes it. rollback discards pending changes in the session. group related work into one commit.. In practical terms, how operations move from in-memory to durable state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Transaction Semantics
Concepts
  • flush: send SQL to DB, keep transaction open.
  • commit: flush then finalize transaction.
  • rollback: discard pending changes in current session.
Practical rule
Group related operations and commit once. Use rollback to recover from exceptions and avoid leaving partial state.
Example sequence
with Session() as session:
  session.add_many_objects(...)
  session.flush()  # IDs assigned, but transaction still open
  # validate data
  session.commit() # finalizes changes

# On error
with Session() as session:
  try:
    do_changes()
    session.commit()
  except Exception:
    session.rollback()
Key Takeaway

Understand flush vs commit. Use rollback on exceptions, and group operations into coherent transactional units for correctness and performance.

screens.title: Session lifecycle pitfalls and detached objects
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most frequent sources of bugs is confusing session-attached objects with detached ones. An object is attached to the Session that loaded or added it. When that session closes, the object becomes detached and further modifications won't be tracked unless you merge it into a new session or requery it. A typical problem occurs when you query an object in one request, close the session, and then attempt to update and commit it in a different session — changes are not persisted unless you explicitly reattach. The remedy is to either perform read-modify-write cycles within a single session or use session. merge to re-associate the detached state. Another issue is leaving sessions open and exhausting the connection pool; always use with Session() to scope sessions and ensure closure. Finally, avoid mixing objects from different sessions in the same transaction. Keep clear boundaries: decide where the session begins and ends, and stick to that pattern to prevent subtle bugs and connection leaks. Session lifecycle pitfalls and detached objects means do work in a single session or merge detached instances into a live session. use with blocks to avoid connection leaks and mixed-session confusion.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.6 › Detached Objects & Lifecycle
Why detachment happens

When a session closes, objects it returned become detached. Detached objects are not tracked for changes by any active session until reattached or merged.

Solutions
  • Keep read-modify-write in one session where possible.
  • Use session.merge(detached_obj) to attach state to a new session.
  • Use with Session() to scope sessions and avoid leaks.
merge example
detached = get_user_somehow()
with Session() as session:
  merged = session.merge(detached)
  merged.email = 'new@example.com'
  session.commit()
Key Takeaway

Design session boundaries deliberately. Reattach detached objects with merge or keep operations in one session to maintain consistent behavior.

screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize three essential concepts. First, the SQLAlchemy ORM maps Python classes to database tables using a declarative base; define columns as class attributes and call Base. metadata. create_all to create tables during development. Second, the Session is the transactional unit of work — create sessions with sessionmaker, stage changes with add or add_all, and finalize with commit; use rollback on error and prefer with blocks to ensure closure. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll make the shift from SQLAlchemy Core's table-and-column world to the ORM, where rows are ordinary Python objects. You'll learn why mapping classes to tables speeds development, how declarative_base establishes that mapping, and how the Session manages a unit of work so your object changes become S Q L transactions. We'll walk through defining a simple User model, creating tables from models, and then performing the full CRUD lifecycle — add, query, update, and delete — all with safe session management. Along the way we'll surface common misconceptions: thinking a queried object is magically persistent across separate sessions, or relying on flush without a commit. By the end you'll be comfortable creating models, using sessionmaker, and grouping related operations into a single transaction. A short hands-on activity will ask you to implement a Book model and exercise one CRUD operation so you can practice the pattern with an SQLite file. This foundation prepares you for relationships and richer object graphs in later chapters. Ready to translate S Q L into objects and write clearer, more maintainable database code?

These objectives focus your work with SQLAlchemy's ORM. First, you'll be able to name the difference between Core and ORM and explain why ORM improves developer productivity by mapping rows to objects. Second, you'll define Python classes as ORM models using declarative_base, including columns and tablename so your classes match the database layout. Third, you'll create and use a Session via sessionmaker to stage changes and run transactional work, knowing when to commit or rollback. Finally, you'll practice CRUD: add new model instances, query them with filter and get calls, update attributes to generate update statements, and delete records safely. For each objective you'll both read and run example code and verify results, so you not only understand the A P I but also can reason about session scope and state. These skills matter because they let you organize data logic in Python, avoid repetitive S Q L, and reduce bugs tied to improper session handling.

You will apply objectives through short code runs and verification checks. For model definition you'll create a User class with id, name, and email, run Base. metadata. create_all, and inspect the resulting table. For sessions you'll use sessionmaker bound to an engine and wrap operations in a with block to ensure closure. For CRUD you'll add single and multiple instances, commit to persist changes, then run queries to verify that new objects have been assigned primary keys. For updates you'll change an attribute on a queried object and commit to see the UPDATE emitted. For deletes you'll mark an object for deletion, commit, and confirm absence with a follow-up query. Each exercise ends with a printed verification so you can see the returned objects and confirm database state. These practice steps remove guesswork and prepare you for multi-model relationships where consistent session patterns are essential.

Start by clarifying the practical difference between Core and ORM. SQLAlchemy Core exposes tables, columns, and S Q L expressions; you construct SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE with engine-level execution. The ORM layers an object mapping on top: Python classes become table blueprints and instances represent rows. Use Core when you need fine-grained S Q L control, complex multi-table expressions, or want to stay close to S Q L. Use ORM when you prefer to manipulate Python objects, encapsulate domain logic in classes, and reduce repetitive S Q L. A common example: inserting many rows with Core can be efficient for bulk operations, while ORM is clearer for a domain model where business rules belong on class methods. Watch for a misconception: ORM does not replace S Q L — understanding generated S Q L helps debug performance. A good habit is to inspect emitted S Q L during development to ensure queries are optimal. The declarative base is the foundation of the ORM mapping. Calling declarative_base produces a Base class that collects metadata and mapping information. When your model classes inherit from this Base and set tablename and Column attributes, SQLAlchemy registers the mapping between Python attributes and table columns. Concretely, you declare id as a Column with Integer and primary_key=True and name as a Column with String and not-null constraints; these definitions are both Python attributes and schema descriptors. One practical effect: when you call Base. metadata. create_all(engine), SQLAlchemy inspects the registered metadata and creates tables for each mapped class. A useful example is a User class with id, name, and email; after you instantiate Base and define User, creating tables is a one-line call. A common misconception is that simply defining classes writes tables — you must call create_all or use migrations to apply schema. Also remember that Column objects belong to class attributes, not instance attributes; instances receive values at runtime. The Session is the ORM's conversation partner for the database. It tracks object state, stages new objects for insertion, notes attribute changes for updates, and marks objects for deletion. To obtain sessions you create a sessionmaker factory bound to an engine; calling that factory returns a new Session instance. Treat a session as a short-lived unit of work: open it, perform related operations, then commit or rollback and close it. The best practice is to use the with-statement so Python closes the session automatically even if an exception occurs. This pattern prevents connection leaks and makes error handling explicit. Remember the difference between flush and commit: flush writes pending S Q L to the database but keeps the transaction open; commit finalizes the transaction. A typical pattern is to add or modify several objects, call commit once, and then verify results. A misconception is assuming objects are sessionless — objects are attached to a session and carrying them across sessions without merging will produce errors or detached states. Always be explicit about session boundaries. Updating records in the ORM is intentionally simple because the Session tracks object state. Query the object you want to change, set new attribute values on the instance, then commit the session. SQLAlchemy will detect the attribute change and emit an UPDATE for the changed columns during flush. For example, find Bob by name, assign a new email value, and then call commit. After committing, a follow-up query verifies the persisted change. A common error is attempting to update an object that was queried in a different, now-closed session without reattaching it. In that case, either requery the object in the new session or merge the detached object. Another pitfall is making assumptions about transactional boundaries: changes remain local to the session until you commit. If you need atomic updates across multiple related objects, perform them inside the same session and then commit once so all changes succeed or all roll back together. This approach keeps your data consistent and your code easier to reason about. To remove rows via the ORM, query the instance you want deleted, call session. delete(instance), then commit. Deletion marks the object for removal, and commit finalizes the change. Always perform a follow-up query to verify the row no longer exists. Understanding transaction semantics is vital. session. flush sends pending S Q L statements to the database without finalizing the transaction. It allows the database to assign values, like auto-incremented IDs, so your in-memory objects receive those values. session. commit flushes and then commits the transaction, making changes permanent. If an error occurs, session. rollback undoes pending changes in that session, returning a clean transactional state. A common mistake is expecting flush to make data durable — it does not; an uncommitted transaction can still be rolled back. Another mistake is calling commit too frequently: many small commits hurt throughput and increase overhead. The practical pattern is to group related changes into a single commit after successful validation. One of the most frequent sources of bugs is confusing session-attached objects with detached ones. An object is attached to the Session that loaded or added it. When that session closes, the object becomes detached and further modifications won't be tracked unless you merge it into a new session or requery it. A typical problem occurs when you query an object in one request, close the session, and then attempt to update and commit it in a different session — changes are not persisted unless you explicitly reattach. The remedy is to either perform read-modify-write cycles within a single session or use session. merge to re-associate the detached state. Another issue is leaving sessions open and exhausting the connection pool; always use with Session() to scope sessions and ensure closure. Finally, avoid mixing objects from different sessions in the same transaction. Keep clear boundaries: decide where the session begins and ends, and stick to that pattern to prevent subtle bugs and connection leaks. Let's summarize three essential concepts. First, the SQLAlchemy ORM maps Python classes to database tables using a declarative base; define columns as class attributes and call Base. metadata. create_all to create tables during development. Second, the Session is the transactional unit of work — create sessions with sessionmaker, stage changes with add or add_all, and finalize with commit; use rollback on error and prefer with blocks to ensure closure. Third, basic CRUD with the ORM is straightforward: add instances to create, query with get/query/filter to read, change attributes on attached instances to update, and use session. delete to remove rows — always verify results with follow-up queries. Keep in mind common pitfalls: detached objects lose tracking once their session closes, flush is not commit, and commit frequency impacts performance. These ideas form the foundation for working with relationships and more advanced ORM features in later chapters.

A short quick-reference to keep handy. Remember to call declarative_base and set tablename for each model. Use sessionmaker bound to your engine and prefer with Session() as session to scope work. After adding or deleting objects, always commit to persist changes; use rollback in exception handlers. For queries, start with session. get for primary-key lookups and use query/filter/filter_by for conditionals. Finally, avoid crossing session boundaries with live objects — either requery or merge detached objects into a new session. These reminders help you write consistent, maintainable ORM code day to day.
